versions.question: In the AWS shared responsibility model, which task is the customer's job for IAM rather than AWS's?
options: Patching the servers that run the IAM service
Setting role permissions and enabling MFA for users
Securing the data centers that host IAM's backend
Operating the global network that IAM requests travel over
versions.explanation: AWS runs the IAM service and the infrastructure under it. The customer configures identities, permissions, MFA and key hygiene.

versions.question: Your auditor asks who must rotate IAM access keys and review overly broad policies. What is the answer?
options: AWS, because IAM is a fully managed service it operates end to end
The customer, since they configure and secure their own IAM setup
AWS Support, whenever a customer opens a case about their keys
The staff running the Region's data centers, as part of facility security
versions.explanation: Security *in* the cloud, including IAM users, policies, MFA and key rotation, belongs to the customer; AWS secures the service itself.

versions.question: Which of these is a valid way to organise IAM users with groups?
options: Nest a Developers group inside an Everyone group
Add the same user to both a Developers and a Billing group
Add an IAM role as a member of a group
Require each user to be placed in a single group before sign-in
versions.explanation: A user may be in several groups (or none). Groups contain users only, not other groups or roles.

versions.question: Alice needs permissions from both the Auditors and the Developers policies. What is true about groups here?
options: She must be in just one group, so a merged group is needed
Groups cannot hold users, only roles
She can be a member of both groups at once
Group membership is limited to one group per Region
versions.explanation: IAM users can belong to multiple groups and receive the union of permissions. Groups hold users only and cannot be nested.

versions.question: You need near-real-time access logs for a CloudFront distribution. Where does CloudFront send the records directly?
options: An Amazon Kinesis data stream
An Amazon OpenSearch Service domain
A CloudWatch Logs log group
An S3 bucket you pick as the destination
versions.explanation: Real-time logs go only to a Kinesis data stream. Firehose or Lambda can then forward them to S3, OpenSearch and so on.

versions.question: A team wants CloudFront real-time logs in S3. Which design is correct?
options: Point the real-time log configuration straight at the bucket
Deliver to a Kinesis data stream, then add Firehose to S3
Enable CloudWatch Logs delivery, then run Athena on it
Send logs to an RDS database and export a nightly dump to S3
versions.explanation: The only direct target is a Kinesis data stream; Firehose sits after the stream to reach S3.

versions.question: A file system's I/O is spiky: idle for hours, then sudden heavy demand. Which EFS throughput mode fits best without capacity planning?
options: Elastic throughput, which scales up and down automatically
Provisioned throughput at your estimated peak, billed continuously
Bursting throughput, tied to the amount of data stored
General Purpose, which is a performance mode that sets IOPS limits
versions.explanation: Elastic mode adapts automatically and is recommended for unpredictable workloads.

versions.question: With which EFS throughput mode does throughput scale with the data stored, so a small file system gets little baseline?
options: Elastic throughput, adjusting up and down on demand
Bursting, with a baseline tied to stored data size
Provisioned throughput, a fixed rate you buy in advance
versions.explanation: Bursting throughput grows with storage size. Provisioned is fixed and paid for; Elastic scales automatically.

versions.question: Dozens of applications share one S3 bucket and each needs its own narrow permissions. What reduces the policy complexity?
options: Create S3 Access Points, each with its own policy and hostname
Add one huge statement list to the single bucket policy
Replicate the bucket into a copy for every application
Use S3 Select to filter what each team can see
versions.explanation: Access points give every application a dedicated endpoint and policy, keeping the bucket policy short.

versions.question: Which S3 feature provides a unique DNS name with its own access policy for a team working on a shared dataset?
options: S3 Inventory reports listing objects and their metadata daily
S3 Access Points, each with a DNS name and its own policy
S3 Batch Operations jobs that run bulk actions on objects
S3 Storage Lens dashboards summarising usage across accounts
versions.explanation: Each access point has its own DNS name and a policy that resembles a bucket policy.

versions.question: A fleet in private subnets needs outbound HTTPS to download packages, yet no inbound connection from the internet may be possible. Which setup works?
options: Place an Elastic IP on every instance and open all inbound ports
Add a NAT gateway in a public subnet and route private traffic to it
Create a VPC peering link to a partner VPC and use its internet gateway
Attach an internet gateway and route 0.0.0.0/0 from the private subnets straight to it
versions.explanation: A NAT gateway in a public subnet forwards outbound traffic via the IGW and only lets replies back.

versions.question: What is the role of a NAT gateway in a VPC?
options: It lets internet users open connections to private instances
It encrypts traffic between an office and the VPC
It gives private subnets outbound-only internet access
It filters traffic at the subnet boundary using stateless rules
versions.explanation: Private instances reach the internet through the NAT gateway in a public subnet; the internet cannot initiate connections inward.

versions.question: Compliance wants customer-controlled encryption keys for S3 objects, with every use of the key recorded in CloudTrail. Which encryption fits?
options: SSE-KMS with a key you manage in AWS KMS
Encryption using keys that S3 creates and owns itself
Encryption with a key the client uploads for each call
Relying on a private bucket ACL alone for protection
versions.explanation: SSE-KMS lets you manage the key, and KMS usage is logged in CloudTrail.

versions.question: Which S3 server-side encryption option requires the reader to have permission on both the object and a KMS key?
options: SSE-S3, where S3 owns and rotates the encryption keys itself
SSE-C, where the caller supplies the key with every request
SSE-KMS, which also checks permissions on a KMS key
Client-side encryption performed before the upload
versions.explanation: With SSE-KMS (header `aws:kms`) decryption goes through KMS, so key permissions are checked too.

versions.question: Which are valid CloudFront invalidation path specifications? (Choose two)
options: /index.html
bucket-name/images/
arn:aws:s3:::site/*
/css/*
versions.explanation: Invalidations take URL paths starting with `/`, for single objects or with a wildcard for a prefix.

versions.question: Which are valid CloudFront invalidation paths for removing specific cached content? (Choose two)
options: /assets/*
/downloads/report.pdf
s3://site-bucket/assets
https://example.com/*.png?x
versions.explanation: Invalidation paths start with `/` and may name a single object or end in a wildcard; URIs and full URLs are not accepted.

versions.question: Which statement describes Route 53 acting as an authoritative DNS service?
options: It caches answers to speed up lookups for end users
It holds the real records for your zones, which you manage
It forwards each query to the root servers
It balances connections across servers using health-aware proxies
versions.explanation: Authoritative means customers control the records; Route 53 returns the definitive answer.

versions.question: A teammate says Route 53 is 'authoritative'. What does that give you?
options: Control over the DNS records for your zones
Ownership of the top-level domain registry
A recursive resolver for your office network
Automatic TCP load balancing across instances
versions.explanation: An authoritative DNS server answers with records the customer manages.

versions.question: Which two statements about CloudFront signed URLs and S3 pre-signed URLs are correct? (Choose two)
options: CloudFront signed URLs can protect content from any origin and benefit from edge caching
A pre-signed S3 URL carries the access rights of whoever created the signature
Pre-signed S3 URLs are validated by CloudFront before reaching an OAC-protected bucket
Viewers of a CloudFront signed URL must hold IAM users
versions.explanation: Use CloudFront signed URLs when distributing via CloudFront; pre-signed URLs go directly to S3 and inherit the signer's permissions.

versions.question: Pick the two true statements. (Choose two)
options: Viewers need AWS credentials to use a CloudFront signed URL
A CloudFront signed URL is usable with S3 or custom HTTP origins and keeps edge caching
S3 pre-signed URLs let the holder act with the signing identity's permissions for a limited time
S3 pre-signed URLs are cached at edge locations by default
versions.explanation: CloudFront signed URLs are origin-agnostic and cached; pre-signed URLs delegate the signer's permissions.

versions.question: Aurora replicas are added and removed by Auto Scaling. Which connection target should read-only clients use?
options: Point clients at the cluster's reader endpoint
A hard-coded list of instance endpoints
The cluster writer endpoint
A Route 53 weighted record per replica, updated by hand
versions.explanation: The reader endpoint tracks the current replicas and spreads connections among them.

versions.question: What does the Aurora reader endpoint do?
options: Sends every statement to the primary instance
Spreads connections over the current replicas
Splits each SQL statement across replicas
Replicates storage to a second AWS Region continuously
versions.explanation: It balances at connection level across the replicas, even as they come and go.

versions.question: A principal from a different AWS account needs GetObject on your bucket. Which configuration is required in your account?
options: A bucket policy naming the external account or principal
A new IAM role for S3 to assume in the other account
Cross-Region replication to the other account
A VPC endpoint policy on the bucket
versions.explanation: Cross-account access needs a resource-based policy on the bucket allowing the other account (plus identity permission there).

versions.question: Which is the standard way to let another account's role read objects in your S3 bucket?
options: Share your root credentials with them
Add a bucket policy allowing their role
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket
Tag the objects with their account ID
versions.explanation: The bucket policy is the resource policy granting cross-account access.

versions.question: How many Availability Zones does a typical new AWS Region have?
options: Usually three, sometimes more
Always exactly two
One for each country served
Exactly one, plus edge locations
versions.explanation: Regions generally have at least 3 AZs, and some have up to 6.

versions.question: Which description of an Availability Zone is accurate?
options: A single rack inside a shared data hall
Isolated data centers with their own power and networking
A CloudFront edge location that caches content near viewers
A logical grouping of accounts within an organisation
versions.explanation: AZs are isolated from each other for fault tolerance yet connected with fast networking, which enables multi-AZ designs.

versions.question: You run a live site and a warm standby elsewhere. Route 53 should answer with the standby only when the live endpoint fails its checks. Which routing policy?
options: Failover routing with a secondary standby record
Geoproximity routing with a bias toward the standby
Simple routing returning both endpoint addresses
Latency-based routing to the lowest-latency Region
versions.explanation: Failover routing has a primary and a secondary and uses health checks to switch.

versions.question: In Route 53 failover routing, what triggers an answer pointing to the secondary record?
options: The primary's health check fails
The secondary has lower latency
A user in a different continent queries
The primary record's weight reaches zero
versions.explanation: Route 53 returns the secondary only when the primary is deemed unhealthy.

versions.question: Database backups are read once or twice a year, need millisecond access when requested, and must tolerate losing an entire AZ. Which storage class?
options: Flexible Retrieval archive, restoring in minutes to hours
Standard-IA, spread over several AZs with rapid access
One Zone-IA, keeping the single copy in one AZ
Deep Archive, restoring within twelve hours or more
versions.explanation: Standard-IA stores across multiple AZs with rapid access at a lower storage price.

versions.question: Which class suits data that is infrequently accessed, needs rapid retrieval, and must be resilient to an AZ outage?
options: Infrequent Access spread over multiple AZs
Infrequent Access held in a single AZ
Archive class with hours-long restores
Express One Zone for single-digit millisecond compute-adjacent access
versions.explanation: Standard-IA keeps data in at least three AZs and retrieves immediately.

versions.question: Geolocation records exist for Europe and Canada. A visitor from Brazil receives no DNS answer. What should be added?
options: A default location record
A longer TTL on the Europe record
An alias to CloudFront
A failover secondary record
versions.explanation: A Default geolocation record handles locations that match no other record.

versions.question: Which Route 53 record covers users whose location doesn't match any geolocation rule you created?
options: Geoproximity bias of 0
A Default location record
Weighted record with weight 255
Multi-value answer
versions.explanation: Without a Default record, unmatched locations get no answer.

versions.question:
Given this lifecycle configuration, what happens to a `logs/` object that is 120 days old?

```json
{"Rules":[{"ID":"logs-tiering","Filter":{"Prefix":"logs/"},"Status":"Enabled","Transitions":[{"Days":30,"StorageClass":"STANDARD_IA"},{"Days":90,"StorageClass":"GLACIER"}],"Expiration":{"Days":365},"AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload":{"DaysAfterInitiation":7}}]}
```
options: It was deleted at day 90 when the Glacier transition ran
It moved to Glacier at day 90 after Standard-IA at day 30
It is still in S3 Standard and untouched by any rule
It moved to Deep Archive at day 120 as the last tier
versions.explanation: Transitions: Standard-IA at 30 days, Glacier at 90 days, and expiry only at 365 days.

versions.question:
Which statement about this lifecycle rule is correct?

```json
{"Rules":[{"ID":"logs-tiering","Filter":{"Prefix":"logs/"},"Status":"Enabled","Transitions":[{"Days":30,"StorageClass":"STANDARD_IA"},{"Days":90,"StorageClass":"GLACIER"}],"Expiration":{"Days":365},"AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload":{"DaysAfterInitiation":7}}]}
```
options: Every object in the bucket is deleted after one year, whatever its prefix
Matching objects expire at 365 days and stale uploads end after 7
Only multipart parts older than 365 days are removed from the bucket
Objects go to Glacier at day 30 and to Standard-IA at day 90
versions.explanation: Scope is the `logs/` prefix: expiration at 365 days, plus aborting incomplete multipart uploads 7 days after initiation. Tiering is IA at 30 and Glacier at 90.

versions.question: A web tier keeps login state in each instance's memory, and users are logged out whenever the load balancer picks another target. What is the quickest fix?
options: Turn on stickiness for the target group
Add more instances to the group
Lower the health-check interval
Move the instances to a single larger type
versions.explanation: Stickiness routes a client's requests to the same target. Externalising sessions to ElastiCache or DynamoDB is the better long-term fix.

versions.question: What is a downside of using sticky sessions with a load balancer?
options: It disables health checks on the target group
It can leave load uneven across targets
It breaks HTTPS listeners
It limits the group to a single Availability Zone only
versions.explanation: Because clients stay on one target, traffic may become unbalanced.

versions.question: Aurora's quorum model keeps six copies across three AZs. How many copies must acknowledge a write?
options: Four of six
Two of six
Six of six
Three of six
versions.explanation: Writes need 4 of 6 and reads need 3 of 6, so Aurora survives an AZ loss.

versions.question: How many of Aurora's six storage copies are needed to serve a read quorum?
options: Four of the six copies
Three of six copies
Two of the six copies
Five of the six copies
versions.explanation: Read quorum is 3 of 6; write quorum is 4 of 6.

versions.question: Data is spread evenly over 10 prefixes in a bucket. What GET/HEAD throughput can the bucket support in theory?
options: About 55,000 requests per second
5,500 requests per second in total
Roughly 30,000 requests per second
A limit of 3,500 for the whole bucket
versions.explanation: Each prefix supports 5,500 GET/HEAD per second, so 10 prefixes give 55,000.

versions.question: Per prefix, what is the baseline S3 read request rate?
options: 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second
3,500 GET/HEAD requests per second, as for writes
A few hundred requests per second
Unlimited, with no per-prefix baseline
versions.explanation: S3 scales to at least 5,500 GET/HEAD per second per prefix (and 3,500 PUT/POST/DELETE).

versions.question: What does running `aws configure` do?
options: Prompts for credentials, Region and format, saving them in ~/.aws
Creates a new IAM user and prints its secret access key afterwards
Attaches an instance profile to the instance you are logged in to
Validates the CLI installation by listing your S3 buckets
versions.explanation: `aws configure` asks for the access key ID, secret key, default Region and output format and writes them to `~/.aws/credentials` and `~/.aws/config`. On EC2 use an IAM role instead.

versions.question: After you answer the `aws configure` prompts, which files hold your settings?
options: ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.aws/config
/etc/aws/keys.json and /etc/aws/region
~/.ssh/id_rsa and ~/.ssh/config
~/.kube/config and ~/.docker/config.json
versions.explanation: The CLI stores keys in `~/.aws/credentials` and Region/output in `~/.aws/config`.

versions.question: A URL to a private S3 object contains `X-Amz-Algorithm`, `X-Amz-Credential`, `X-Amz-Signature` and `X-Amz-Expires`. What kind of link is it?
options: A time-limited pre-signed URL
A CloudFront origin URL
A permanent public link
A Transfer Acceleration endpoint
versions.explanation: These query parameters belong to a SigV4 pre-signed URL that stops working after expiry.

versions.question: What does `X-Amz-Expires` in an S3 URL indicate?
options: The date the object will be deleted by lifecycle
How long the signed link stays valid
The CloudFront cache TTL
The age of the signing key before rotation
versions.explanation: It is the validity period of a pre-signed URL.

versions.question: An Auto Scaling group's launch template now references a patched AMI. How can the running instances be swapped in a rolling manner while keeping capacity?
options: Start an instance refresh and set a minimum healthy percentage
Detach every instance manually and re-attach
Switch the termination policy to OldestInstance and wait
Raise the maximum size and delete the old ones
versions.explanation: Instance refresh replaces instances in batches, respecting the minimum healthy percentage and warm-up.

versions.question: Which Auto Scaling feature gradually replaces instances after a launch template change?
options: Scheduled actions
Instance refresh
Lifecycle hooks on launch
Predictive scaling
versions.explanation: Instance refresh does a rolling replacement controlled by minimum healthy % and warm-up time.

versions.question: Two viewers request `https://d111.cloudfront.net/logo.png`. With the default cache settings, what identifies the cached object?
options: The domain name and the URL path
Domain, path and every cookie sent by the viewer
The viewer's User-Agent header
The file's ETag from the origin
versions.explanation: By default the cache key is hostname plus path; headers, cookies and query strings are added only if configured.

versions.question: Which of these is included in a CloudFront cache key only if you add it to the cache policy?
options: The distribution's domain name
The object's URL path
A cookie sent by the viewer
versions.explanation: The default cache key is hostname plus path. Cookies, headers and query strings are added only when configured.

versions.question: Route 53 uses about 15 global checkers to monitor an endpoint. When does it mark the endpoint healthy?
options: When more than 18% of checkers report success
Only if every checker sees a response
When a single checker passes
When DNS resolves the endpoint's name
versions.explanation: An endpoint is healthy if more than 18% of the checkers say it is.

versions.question: Which statement about Route 53 health checks is correct?
options: Checks pass only when the endpoint answers with exactly HTTP 200
HTTP, HTTPS and TCP checks are possible; 2xx/3xx passes
They cannot inspect the response body at all, only status codes
Checkers always run from the endpoint's own Region only
versions.explanation: Pass means 2xx/3xx; you can also match text in the first 5,120 bytes and choose checker locations.

versions.question: Your assets bucket must not be publicly readable, but users should fetch them via a CloudFront distribution. What is the recommended configuration?
options: Use OAC and trust the distribution in the bucket policy
An S3 bucket ACL granting AllUsers read access to every object
The bucket's website endpoint with public read permissions
An IAM user's long-term keys embedded in the distribution origin
versions.explanation: OAC lets only CloudFront sign requests to S3; direct S3 URLs are denied.

versions.question: What is the effect of using OAC for an S3 origin?
options: Direct S3 URLs are denied; the CloudFront URL still works
The bucket must be made public before CloudFront can read it
CloudFront caching is switched off for that origin entirely
Every request is tunnelled through a Site-to-Site VPN
versions.explanation: The bucket policy trusts the CloudFront service principal for that distribution only.

versions.question: Replica copies of data that can be regenerated need cheap infrequent-access storage with millisecond retrieval, and AZ loss is acceptable. Which class?
options: Standard-IA, with copies in three or more AZs
One Zone-IA, a single-AZ copy at a lower price
Glacier Flexible Retrieval, with restores taking minutes to hours
Intelligent-Tiering, with automatic access tiers and a monitoring fee
versions.explanation: One Zone-IA is cheaper because it stores in a single AZ; it suits recreatable data or secondary copies.

versions.question: What is the main trade-off of S3 One Zone-IA compared with Standard-IA?
options: Objects must be restored before they can be read
Cheaper, because data lives in only one AZ
A 5 TB minimum object size for every object stored
Server-side encryption cannot be enabled on the bucket
versions.explanation: Data is stored in a single AZ, which lowers cost but loses AZ resilience.

versions.question: Which are Route 53 health check types? (Choose three)
options: A check that reads an SQS queue depth directly
A check of a public endpoint by IP or domain
A check that aggregates results of other checks with AND/OR logic
A check driven by the state of a CloudWatch alarm
A check that logs in to each host over RDP
versions.explanation: Types are endpoint, calculated and CloudWatch alarm health checks.

versions.question: Which three describe valid Route 53 health checks? (Choose three)
options: Monitoring an AWS resource or server endpoint
Combining other checks into a parent check
Following the status of a CloudWatch alarm
Scanning an EBS volume for bad blocks
Running a Lambda function every hour on a schedule
versions.explanation: Endpoint, calculated and CloudWatch alarm checks are the supported kinds.

versions.question: Configuring S3 event notifications to deliver to an SQS queue fails with an access error. What fixes it?
options: Add a resource policy on the queue letting S3 send messages
Create an IAM user for the bucket and place its keys in the queue settings
Enable versioning on the bucket so events can be queued
Allow the queue's ARN in the bucket's CORS configuration
versions.explanation: SQS needs an access policy trusting S3; SNS and Lambda need analogous resource policies.

versions.question: Which resource-based policy do S3 event notifications to Lambda require?
options: A bucket ACL granting the Lambda execution role access
A Lambda resource-based policy letting S3 invoke it
A KMS grant naming the S3 bucket as grantee principal
A security group rule on the function's network interface
versions.explanation: Each event destination needs a resource policy allowing the S3 service to deliver events.

versions.question: When an S3 bucket's website endpoint is used as a CloudFront origin, how does CloudFront classify it?
options: As a custom (HTTP) origin
As an S3 origin using OAC
As a MediaStore origin
As a Lambda function URL origin
versions.explanation: The website endpoint is an HTTP server, so it is a custom origin and cannot use OAC.

versions.question: Which limitation applies to an S3 static website endpoint behind CloudFront?
options: It must be configured as an S3 origin with OAC enabled
It's a custom origin, so OAC cannot be applied
It has to live in us-east-1 to work with CloudFront
It cannot serve index documents through CloudFront
versions.explanation: Website endpoints are custom origins; OAC works with the S3 REST API endpoint.

versions.question: An instance has a role attached. What gets the temporary credentials from the instance metadata service?
options: The SDK's default credential chain and the CLI
The EC2 console, which pastes them to you
The VPC route table
An access key you create and bake into the AMI
versions.explanation: SDKs and the CLI fetch role credentials from IMDS automatically.

versions.question: Why do you not need to store keys on an EC2 instance that has an IAM role?
options: Instances are exempt from IAM authorisation checks
The SDK pulls rotating keys from the metadata service
Security groups sign API calls on the instance's behalf
Roles turn off the need for any authentication
versions.explanation: The SDK retrieves and refreshes role credentials from IMDS.

versions.question: Which two practices follow IAM best practice for a new team? (Choose two)
options: Give every user AdministratorAccess to avoid support tickets
Grant only the permissions a person's tasks require
Attach permissions to groups that mirror job functions
Use the root account for day-to-day work
versions.explanation: Least privilege and group-based management are core IAM guidelines.

versions.question: Which two actions are recommended when managing human access in AWS? (Choose two)
options: Give each person an individual identity rather than shared credentials
Put users in groups and attach policies to the groups
Share one access key pair across the team for simplicity
Use root credentials for daily admin tasks
versions.explanation: One identity per person and group-based permissions are best practice, alongside least privilege and a locked-down root user.

versions.question: A bucket policy allows `s3:GetObject` to `*`, yet anonymous requests are refused. What should you check first?
options: Block Public Access is on for the bucket or account
Object Lock is set in compliance mode on the bucket
Transfer Acceleration is switched on for the bucket
A lifecycle rule has expired the newest object versions
versions.explanation: Block Public Access overrides public policies and ACLs.

versions.question: Which S3 setting can override a public-read bucket policy and, if enabled at account level, affects all buckets?
options: Object Lock
Block Public Access
Requester Pays
Intelligent-Tiering archive access
versions.explanation: Block Public Access is a safety net against accidental exposure.

versions.question: Occasional ThrottlingException responses occur from an AWS API in your code. Which strategy is recommended?
options: Retry with exponentially growing waits
Immediately file a quota increase request
Switch to another Region on every error
Stop calling the API until support responds
versions.explanation: Exponential backoff handles intermittent throttling; sustained throttling calls for a quota increase.

versions.question: When should you request a service quota increase rather than rely on backoff?
options: When one throttled call happens after a burst
When normal workload keeps exceeding the quota
When one call times out on a flaky network
When the SDK version is a few releases old
versions.explanation: Constant throttling reflects a real shortage of quota; occasional bursts are handled by exponential backoff.

versions.question: Name resolution for `db.corp.internal` should work only for resources inside certain VPCs. Which Route 53 resource do you set up?
options: Private hosted zone associated with those VPCs
Public hosted zone with restricted ACLs
Resolver inbound endpoint alone for the internet
Traffic policy with geolocation rules
versions.explanation: Private hosted zones answer only inside associated VPCs.

versions.question: What is the difference between public and private Route 53 hosted zones?
options: Private zones answer only within associated VPCs
Public zones can only hold alias records, never A records
Private zones are free of charge while public ones cost money
Public zones are limited to one Region of your choice
versions.explanation: Private hosted zones are not visible from the internet.

versions.question: Which two services are reachable through a Gateway VPC endpoint? (Choose two)
options: Amazon DynamoDB tables
Amazon SNS topics
Amazon S3 buckets
AWS Secrets Manager secrets
versions.explanation: Only S3 and DynamoDB use gateway endpoints, implemented as route table targets.

versions.question: Which two statements describe a Gateway VPC endpoint? (Choose two)
options: It is added as a target in route tables
It creates an ENI with a private IP in your subnet
It is supported for S3 and DynamoDB
It is billed per hour and per GB
versions.explanation: Gateway endpoints are free route-table targets for S3 and DynamoDB; interface endpoints use ENIs and are billed.

versions.question: An engineer wonders if the `yum install` in an EC2 user data script needs `sudo`. What is the correct answer?
options: Yes, because commands run under an unprivileged login shell
Only if an instance profile is attached to the instance
No, the script already runs as root at first boot
Yes, because it runs as the ec2-user account
versions.explanation: User data runs once at first launch with root privileges.

versions.question: Which statement about EC2 user data scripts is true?
options: They run on every reboot as ec2-user by default
They run as root during the first boot
They need an IAM role to execute
They can only run Python
versions.explanation: By default user data runs once at first boot as root.

versions.question: Which two can be registered as MFA for an IAM user? (Choose two)
options: A hardware TOTP token
An email link
A passkey or FIDO security key
The account's access key ID
versions.explanation: Supported options include virtual apps, FIDO keys and hardware TOTP tokens.

versions.question: Which two options are supported AWS MFA types? (Choose two)
options: Authenticator app generating TOTP codes
Security question
A hardware security key that supports FIDO2 (WebAuthn)
A CAPTCHA on the sign-in page
versions.explanation: Virtual authenticator apps and FIDO security keys are supported MFA devices.

versions.question: A site team ships `app.v43.js` instead of overwriting `app.js` so users get new code immediately. Why does this work with CloudFront?
options: CloudFront compares the file's checksum with the origin on every request
A new name is a new cache key, forcing a fetch from the origin
Browsers always bypass CloudFront for URLs containing a version
CloudFront automatically invalidates file names that contain a version
versions.explanation: Objects are cached by key (URL), not content. A new name was never cached.

versions.question: Why does reusing the same file name after an update risk stale content at the edge?
options: CloudFront refuses to cache objects that were overwritten at the origin
An unchanged key means the cached copy is served until its TTL ends
S3 locks an object against replacement after the first upload
The edge compares ETags with the origin on every viewer request
versions.explanation: With an unchanged URL the cache key matches the cached object, which is served until it expires.

versions.question: Behind an ALB, your web server's logs show the balancer's address for every request. Which header holds the original client address?
options: X-Forwarded-For
X-Amz-Cf-Id
Via-Client
X-Forwarded-Proto
versions.explanation: ALB adds X-Forwarded-For with the client's IP.

versions.question: How can a target behind an Application Load Balancer determine the originating IP of the caller?
options: It reads the TCP source address of the connection
It reads the X-Forwarded-For header the ALB adds
It queries the ALB's access log API per request
It relies on the target group's stickiness cookie
versions.explanation: The connection comes from the ALB, so the client IP is in the X-Forwarded-For header.

versions.question: Which VPC component is a stateless firewall applied at the subnet level, supporting both allow and deny rules?
options: Security group
Network ACL
VPC endpoint
Flow Logs
versions.explanation: NACLs are stateless, evaluated at the subnet, and have allow and deny rules; security groups are stateful and allow-only.

versions.question: You need to privately connect two VPCs with non-overlapping CIDR ranges, understanding that traffic does not pass through a third VPC. Which component?
options: VPC peering
NAT gateway
Site-to-Site VPN
Gateway endpoint
versions.explanation: Peering links two VPCs privately; it is non-transitive and needs non-overlapping CIDRs.

versions.question: A volume holds archive data touched a few times each year, and the lowest cost per GB matters most. Which EBS volume type?
options: Cold HDD (sc1), the cheapest per GB
General Purpose SSD (gp3) with baseline IOPS
Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) for databases
Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) for big data
versions.explanation: sc1 is the cheapest EBS type, for infrequently accessed data.

versions.question: Which EBS type has the lowest cost per GB for infrequently accessed workloads?
options: gp3, general purpose SSD with tunable IOPS
sc1, cold HDD aimed at archival access
io2, provisioned IOPS SSD for databases
st1, throughput optimised HDD for streaming
versions.explanation: Cold HDD (sc1) is the lowest-cost option.

versions.question: Put the steps in order for a first-time request of an object at a CloudFront edge location that does not have it yet.
items: Viewer's request is routed to a nearby edge location
The edge looks in its cache and finds nothing
The edge sends a request to the configured origin
The origin responds with the object
The edge stores a copy for its TTL and delivers it to the viewer
versions.explanation: On a cache miss the edge fetches from the origin and caches the result; later viewers get a cache hit.

versions.question: What happens on a CloudFront cache miss at an edge location?
options: It fetches from the origin, caches and returns it
The edge returns a 404 to the viewer straight away
The edge asks a neighbouring edge to answer for it
The request waits until the object's TTL has expired
versions.explanation: A miss makes the edge fetch from the origin; the object is then cached for its TTL.

versions.question: What guidance applies to choosing an expiry time for CloudFront signed URLs?
options: Minutes for widely shared links, longer for personal downloads
Set the lifetime to 365 days for every URL, regardless of use
Signed URLs cannot carry an expiry; use cache TTL instead
Always match the lifetime to the object's cache TTL value
versions.explanation: Expiry should reflect how the content is used.

versions.question: A live-event stream link is shared widely. How should its signed URL lifetime be set?
options: Very short, a few minutes at most
Very long, such as several years
No expiry so viewers can return later
Equal to the TTL of the cached object
versions.explanation: Shared content should expire quickly to limit abuse; personal downloads can be valid longer.

versions.question: A new engineer in the Frankfurt Region cannot find a separate list of IAM users there. Why?
options: IAM is global, so identities apply in every Region
IAM data must be replicated to each Region every night
IAM can only be used from the N. Virginia Region
Each Region requires its own separate AWS account
versions.explanation: IAM is a global service; identities apply across Regions.

versions.question: Which statement about IAM and Regions is accurate?
options: Users created in one Region are invisible elsewhere
IAM policies must be duplicated per Region
IAM resources are not tied to a single Region
IAM roles work only in us-east-1
versions.explanation: IAM is global: users, groups, roles and policies apply everywhere.

versions.question: For disaster recovery, a volume's data must be restorable in a different Region. What is the usual approach?
options: Copy a snapshot to the target Region and restore from it
Attach the source volume directly to a remote-Region instance
Mount the volume over NFS from an instance in the original Region
Create a cluster placement group spanning two Regions
versions.explanation: Snapshots can be copied across Regions and restored into new volumes.

versions.question: Which EBS capability supports moving volume data to another Region?
options: Copying snapshots to a different Region
Multi-Attach, sharing a volume among instances
Elastic Volumes, resizing a volume while in use
Fast Snapshot Restore for faster volume creation in an AZ
versions.explanation: Copy the snapshot to the destination Region to recreate the volume there.

versions.question: A 12 GB backup must be uploaded to S3, but a single PUT cannot handle it. Which feature is required?
options: Break it up using multipart upload
Byte-range fetches against the object
S3 Select to read part of the object
Cross-Region replication of the bucket
versions.explanation: Single PUT maxes out at 5 GB; multipart is required above that and recommended above 100 MB.

versions.question: Which advantage does S3 multipart upload provide?
options: Parts upload in parallel; failed parts retry alone
It lifts the 5 TB maximum object size limit
It encrypts the object automatically with SSE-C
It stores each part in a different Region
versions.explanation: Multipart splits objects into parts uploaded in parallel and is needed above 5 GB per object upload.

versions.question: What is true when S3 replication meets deletions in the source bucket? (Choose two)
options: Delete markers may be replicated if you enable that option
Version-specific deletes in the source are not replicated
Every permanent version deletion is copied to the destination
Delete markers are always replicated and cannot be disabled
versions.explanation: Delete marker replication is optional, and deleting a specific version ID is not propagated, protecting the destination.

versions.question: Choose two correct facts about S3 replication behaviour. (Choose two)
options: Delete marker replication can be turned on
Deleting a particular object version in the source does not delete it at the destination
Replication copies deletes of specific versions to avoid drift
Delete markers are never allowed in a replicated bucket
versions.explanation: Version-ID deletes are not replicated; delete markers replicate only when enabled.
